# Product Requirements Document: AI-Enabled Transformation Roadmap Tool (MVP)

Version 0.1 — draft for review — 13 August 2026.

_Prepared for Liv DeSantis, Aberdeen Advisors._

## How to read this document

This is a build-ready specification for a tool that carries a transformation engagement from
charter to living roadmap, replacing the spreadsheet-and-deck pipeline the firm runs today.
It was written from two sources only: the firm's eight-phase transformation methodology, and
one anonymized past engagement whose workbooks and decks were reverse-engineered to recover
the real mechanics — the scoring model, the maturity framework, the taxonomy, and the places
the current process leaks. Nothing here is aspirational feature invention; where the evidence
runs out, the document says so.
Functional requirements are numbered `FR-NNN` and each carries acceptance criteria numbered
`AC-NNN.n`. AI capabilities are numbered `AI-01` to `AI-34` and specified in §8, one
subsection each. Every assumption the specification rests on is collected in §13, and every
question that needs a human answer before build is collected in §14 — read those two first if
you are deciding whether to fund this.

## Source basis and anonymization

Two sources of truth stand behind this document: the eight-phase engagement methodology, and
a single anonymized reference engagement comprising two working spreadsheets, four decks, and
one recap email.
All client-identifying detail has been removed from the reference engagement: the client and
third-party organization names, all personal names, all work email addresses and telephone
numbers, and all client-specific financial figures.
Structural facts have been retained deliberately, because they are the specification: the
three scoring dimensions and their weights, the band and quadrant thresholds, the maturity
level definitions, the shape of the theme and initiative taxonomy, and the observed defects
in the existing workbooks. A structural fact describes the method; it does not identify the
client.

## 1. Purpose, Problem, and Product Thesis

### 1.1 What the product is

This product is a single-workspace system of record for a transformation roadmap engagement: it holds the charter, the evidence, the maturity assessment, the opportunity register, the scoring model, the sequencing, the costs, the value case, and the decisions as versioned structured data rather than as cells and shapes. Every consultant-facing deliverable (maturity heatmap, opportunity landscape, workshop pack, board narrative, activation plan) is generated as a projection of that data, so a number can only appear in a document because it exists, sourced and owned, in the model. Every AI capability in the product is bounded by the propose to review to commit pattern: the AI writes `AISuggestion` records, and a human consultant accepts, edits, or rejects each one before it touches a canonical field.

### 1.2 The problem, stated in the mechanics of the reference engagement

The reference engagement was a roughly twelve-week technology strategy engagement running from interviews through a two-day onsite workshop to a follow-on execution-planning phase. Its entire analytical spine was six files: two Excel workbooks and four PowerPoint decks.

| Artifact | Role in the engagement |
|---|---|
| Master workbook (8 sheets) | CMMI maturity assessment across 28 focus areas, 43-row opportunity register with the full weighted scoring model, quadrant logic, theme definitions, pain-point linkage, reviewer comment threads |
| Client share workbook (7 sheets) | Derived client-facing copy: 43 technology opportunities plus 12 operating-model opportunities, scoring guide, and the only intact copy of the theme/initiative taxonomy (in a hidden sheet) |
| Maturity deck (7 slides) | Eight capability areas plus a four-page CMMI heatmap |
| Onsite deck (67 slides) | Day 1 findings playback and Day 2 workshop instrument |
| Execution-planning deck, dated (23 slides) | Seven initiatives requiring near-term mobilization, plus firm qualifications and case studies |
| Execution-planning deck, working superset (33 slides) | The same 23 slides plus a 10-slide "slide garden" of reusable and other-client material |

Nothing in that stack has an identity, an owner, a version, or a provenance trail. The opportunity register has no ID column at all: an opportunity's identity is the concatenation of its Initiative text and its Opportunity text, so renaming either one silently creates a different opportunity. The taxonomy that the register depends on lives in a hidden sheet inside a *different* file and is reached by external reference. The client-facing copy of the analysis is a save-as of the master, which is why its formulas still point at `[1]Opportunities!$J$5:$N$5`. The judgment that produced each score, and the reasoning behind each sequencing call, survives only as threaded Excel comments addressed to named colleagues, or not at all.

### 1.3 Why Excel plus PowerPoint is the binding constraint

The constraint is not that spreadsheets are imprecise. It is that the analytical logic, the taxonomy, the audit trail, and the deliverable are four separate hand-maintained copies of the same facts, and the tooling cannot detect when they diverge. Six specific defects observed in the reference engagement show the mechanism:

1. **Scores are stored as prose and parsed positionally.** Each of the three scoring dimensions is entered as a full anchor sentence, and the numeric score is recovered with `=VALUE(LEFT(H7,1))` in an adjacent hidden column, replicated 43 times per dimension. The score is therefore whatever character happens to sit in position 1 of a free-text cell. Reordering the anchor text, or pasting a rubric label with a leading space, changes the arithmetic with no visible error.
2. **The weights are hard-coded into a formula row, and there are two copies of them.** The weight triple 0.40 / 0.35 / 0.25 appears once in row 4 and again, interleaved with prose, in row 5. Only the row-5 copy is read, by `=SUMPRODUCT($I$5:$M$5,I7:M7)`, which spans two prose cells and works only because Excel coerces text to zero. Changing the weighting model means editing a row of a spreadsheet and hoping every sheet in every copy was edited the same way. In the share workbook's operating-model sheet, the same SUMPRODUCT reaches the weights through a broken external reference to the other file.
3. **The taxonomy is typed, not enforced.** The initiative picker list is an 18-row column backing 17 real initiatives, because one initiative name appears twice, unmerged. Theme values are resolved by `XLOOKUP` for most rows but hard-typed as literal strings on others, and one theme label carries a stray leading slash while another is misspelled. The result is that the same theme exists under three different names across the two workbooks and the recap email.
4. **Two identity schemes and two score scales coexist in hidden sheets.** The live register has no ID column and 43 rows on a 1 to 5 weighted scale. A hidden sheet carries `OPP-01` through `OPP-27` on an entirely different 8 / 7 / 5 / 4 scale with its own effort grid and priority bands. The two sets do not reconcile one to one, and both were used to talk to the client.
5. **The formulas fall out of alignment and nobody notices.** From row 49 down, the priority-band formula and the business-value formula are one column apart from where they sit in rows 7 to 48: the Priority column holds `=SUM(M49+I49)/2` and the Business Value column holds `=K49`. In the same row, the Status column, which elsewhere holds one of three short enum values, holds a free-text paragraph asking whether a score should be raised.
6. **The deliverable drifts away from the model.** The workshop deck states four themes, roughly twenty initiatives, and roughly fifty opportunities, and gives per-theme counts of 13 / 16 / 19 / 8 with shares of 23% / 29% / 34% / 14%, summing to 56. The workbooks contain 17 initiatives and 43 plus 12 rows. Two deck slides carry a hand-typed footer reading "First draft, will be updated based on additional inputs", which is the only mechanism the stack has for expressing staleness.

Two further defects compound these. Conditional formatting rules across four sheets still test theme names that were retired mid-engagement, so colour on the page encodes a taxonomy that no longer exists. And the working execution-planning deck carries ten slides of another client's material inside the same file as the live client deliverable, which is a confidentiality exposure created purely by the file being the unit of work.

### 1.4 What "one step further than Excel plus PowerPoint" concretely means

Three commitments, each of which directly negates a defect class above.

**A single versioned data model under the analysis.** Every fact has exactly one home, one identity that is not its display text, one owner, and one formula. Scores are integers on a declared `ScoreDimension` with a labelled anchor rubric; the label is rendered from the integer, never parsed out of it. Weights live on a `ScoringModel` record with an effective date, not in a formula row. Theme, Initiative, and Opportunity are enforced referential relationships, so a rename propagates and a duplicate is impossible to create. Derived values (`gap`, `weighted_score`, `priority_band`, `business_value`, `urgency`, `quadrant`, `bubble_size`) are computed by the calculation engine and are not writable, which makes off-by-one-column drift structurally unrepresentable.

**Generated deliverables rather than hand-maintained ones.** The maturity heatmap, the opportunity landscape bubble chart, the four theme slides with their counts and shares, the workshop card set, the board exhibits, and the activation plan are all rendered from the model at a named snapshot. A deliverable records the snapshot it was rendered from, so "the deck says 56 and the workbook says 55" becomes impossible: the deck's counts are the model's counts, and re-rendering is cheap enough that nobody retypes. Client-facing views are permission projections of the same model rather than save-as copies, which removes both the broken-external-reference class and the parked-other-client-material class.

**A roadmap that stays live after delivery.** The recap email issued after the reference workshop explicitly warned that "some of the rankings/scoring on the deck will shift based on further collaboration", and then listed six named refinement workstreams. That warning is a symptom of a stack that cannot express provisionality or reproduce a prior state. In this product, a deliverable issued on a date is reproducible from its snapshot forever; a subsequent edit is a new version with a diff; and the roadmap continues past delivery into `Milestone`, `KPI`, `ActualsSnapshot`, and refresh cycles rather than ending as a PDF.

## 2. Evidence Base and the Current Process, Reverse-Engineered

Everything in this section is observed in the reference engagement's artifacts. Client identity, personnel, and figures are omitted; structure, counts, formula shapes, enum sets, and deck architecture are reproduced exactly, because those are the requirements.

### 2.1 What was examined

| Artifact type | What it contained | Phase served |
|---|---|---|
| Master analysis workbook, 8 sheets, 2 hidden | Introduction and navigation guide; CMMI level definitions calibrated to the client; maturity assessment of 28 focus areas under 8 capability areas with current level, target level, `gap = target - current`, rationale, evidence, gaps, next steps, and a priority-to-fix label; a 43-row opportunity register with 27 columns; a superseded 55-row register retained as a hidden sheet; an initiative picker list on a hidden sheet; a scoring guide with three 5-level anchor rubrics; a theme-definitions sheet holding old and new theme names side by side | Weeks 3 to 4 (maturity and prioritization) |
| Client share workbook, 7 sheets, 4 hidden | A flattened 43-row opportunity view with per-column definition text in a description row; a 12-row operating-model opportunity sheet; the scoring guide; the only intact theme/initiative taxonomy (17 initiatives, each with a sequence number 1 to 4, an optional old name, and a paragraph description); a hidden priority-and-effort heat map on a different ID and score scale; a hidden 5-value status enum list | Weeks 3 to 4 (client-facing share) |
| Standalone maturity deck, 7 slides | Title; the eight capability areas; the CMMI method and level definitions; the heatmap split across four slides | Weeks 3 to 4 (deliverable) |
| Two-day onsite deck, 67 slides | Agenda, objectives, and working agreements; assessment inputs; interview themes across people, process, technology, data; survey strengths; the eight capability areas; the four-part heatmap; "tensions beneath the surface"; an external best-in-class benchmark table with current maturity, a north-star comparator, and attributes per business domain; per-leader deep-dive slides; sponsor strategic goals and guiding principles; the four investment themes with counts and shares; the taxonomy explainer; the scoring explainer; four per-theme slides; the opportunity landscape bubble chart with quadrant call-out lists; foundational elements for the roadmap as seven numbered cards; Day 2 Miro instructions for four activities; wrap-up and next steps | Week 5 equivalent (workshop and V1 roadmap) |
| Recap email, 2 pages | Five synthesized themes; an explicit warning that rankings and scoring will shift; six named next-step workstreams | Post-workshop |
| Execution-planning deck, dated, 23 slides | The readiness-gap framing; a seven-row table of initiatives requiring near-term mobilization with an immediate-readiness focus and a firm-expertise column, five of them starred as having detail slides; five one-per-initiative detail slides; a three-step next-steps timeline; firm qualifications and six case studies | Follow-on scoping |
| Execution-planning deck, working superset, 33 slides | The same 23 slides plus a 10-slide "slide garden" holding reusable and other-client material | Follow-on scoping, working draft |

### 2.2 The as-is workflow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    K["Kickoff, objectives, document request<br/>Week 0"] --> INT["Executive interviews, functional deep dives,<br/>leader strategy sessions, org-wide survey"]
    DOC["Client documents: strategy, architecture,<br/>project lists, budgets, org charts"] --> PP
    INT --> PP["Pain-point inventory<br/>HAND-KEYED into master workbook"]
    PP --> MAT["Maturity sheet: 28 focus areas<br/>current, target, gap = target - current"]
    PP --> OPP["Opportunity register: 43 rows<br/>scores entered as prose anchor sentences"]
    TAX["Themes and Initiatives sheet<br/>hidden, lives in the OTHER workbook"] -.->|"external reference"| OPP
    MAT --> MD["Maturity deck: 4-page heatmap<br/>HAND-BUILT from sheet values"]
    OPP --> CALC["Derived columns: parsed scores, SUMPRODUCT,<br/>priority band, business value, urgency, quadrant"]
    CALC --> ONS["Onsite deck, 67 slides<br/>counts and shares HAND-TYPED"]
    MD --> ONS
    BM["External benchmark research"] --> ONS
    SUR["Survey results"] --> ONS
    ONS --> D1["Day 1: findings playback"]
    D1 --> D2["Day 2: four facilitated Miro activities"]
    D2 --> MIRO["Miro board: top-five cards, urgency dropdowns,<br/>dependency dropdowns, milestones,<br/>t-shirt sizes, roadmap placement, owners"]
    MIRO -->|"HAND-KEYED back as a rank column"| OPP
    D2 --> REC["Recap email: 5 themes, 6 next steps,<br/>warning that rankings will shift"]
    OPP -->|"SAVE-AS copy, links break"| SHARE["Client share workbook<br/>plus 12 operating-model rows scored separately"]
    CALC --> EXEC["Execution-planning deck<br/>7 mobilization initiatives + quals"]
    EXEC --> ACT["Activation: follow-on scope, milestones,<br/>tracking held OUTSIDE every artifact"]
```

There are four hand re-entry points in that flow, and each is a place where the copies can silently diverge: pain points and interview content into the workbook; workbook values into the maturity deck; workbook values into the onsite deck; and workshop output from the Miro board back into the workbook as a client-assigned rank column 1 to 19 that then coexists with the calculated score. There is a fifth leak that is not a re-entry point at all: activation tracking has no home in the stack, so once the execution-planning deck is issued the roadmap stops being a data object.

### 2.3 Where the work actually happens

| Work done in Excel (calculation and bookkeeping) | Work done in PowerPoint (synthesis and judgment) | Work done live in a workshop (facilitation and client commitment) |
|---|---|---|
| Assigning a current level 1 to 5 and a target level 1 to 5 to each of 28 focus areas; computing `gap = target - current`; rendering the level label with `=CHOOSE(F8,"Initial","Managed","Defined","Quantitatively Managed","Optimizing")` | Grouping 28 focus areas into 8 capability areas and choosing that grouping as the client-legible frame | Day 1 findings playback: interview themes, survey strengths, maturity heatmap, tensions beneath the surface, external benchmark, per-leader deep dives, sponsor goals and guiding principles |
| Recording, per focus area, the current-state summary, rationale for the score, evidence and criteria met, gaps, next steps to advance, and a priority-to-fix label | Splitting the 28-row heatmap across four slides so it is readable, and choosing which columns survive the cut | Presenting the four themes with their opportunity counts and percentage shares, and the taxonomy and scoring model, before asking the room to prioritize |
| Holding the 43-row register with theme, initiative, opportunity, recommended action, strategy alignment, three prose scores, three parsed scores, weighted score, priority band, business value, urgency, bubble size, quadrant, "so what", source, status, notes, linked pain points, a foundational flag, relationship type, and the client-assigned top-priority rank | Writing the four theme narratives: a paragraph each explaining why the theme exists and what it buys, which is the single highest-judgment artifact in the engagement | Activity 1, 50 minutes: each group moves its top five critical priorities into a Top Five column from its own card set, reports out for 5 minutes, takes 5 minutes of challenge, then the firm reveals its own ranking and the room reconciles over a 10-minute timer |
| Computing the weighted score as `SUMPRODUCT(weights, scores)` with weights 0.40 financial impact, 0.35 risk if deferred, 0.25 strategic alignment, max 5.0 | Writing each opportunity's "so what": one or two sentences that convert a score into a reason a leader should care | Activity 2, 30 minutes: each group assigns an urgency level to its top five using a dropdown on the card, reports out, and reconciles against the firm's assignment |
| Banding priority with a nested IF at 4.5 Critical, 3.75 High, 2.8 Medium, else Lower | Choosing the bubble-chart encoding: X business value, Y urgency, bubble size weighted score, colour theme; and hand-listing the Act Now and Plan and Fund members beside the chart | Activity 3, 60 minutes: per opportunity, pick dependencies from a dropdown, outline enabling milestones, describe business value, and assign a t-shirt size from a 6-level scale XS to XXL with effort, duration, and risk definitions; then assign owners as a full group |
| Computing `business_value = (alignment + financial) / 2`, `urgency = risk`, `bubble_size = weighted_score`, and the 2x2 quadrant at threshold 3.5 into Act Now / Defend / Plan and Fund / Sequence Later | Declaring the seven "foundational elements for the roadmap" that must be true before sequencing means anything, and the six sequencing inputs split into "focus of today" (priority, dependencies, t-shirt sizing, business value) and "refine later" (resource constraints, cost) | Activity 4, 45 minutes: facilitated full-group placement of each initiative and opportunity onto the roadmap timeline using the priority, urgency, dependency, milestone, and effort inputs from the previous activities |
| Maintaining the taxonomy: 4 themes, 17 initiatives each with a sequence number 1 to 4 and a paragraph description, 43 technology plus 12 operating-model opportunities | Selecting the seven initiatives that require near-term mobilization and writing one detail slide each with scope, readiness focus, and the expertise required | Capturing the room's disagreement: the client-assigned "Identified as Top Priority" rank 1 to 19 came off the board and was keyed into the workbook as a column beside the calculated score, with the two never reconciled |
| Linking opportunities to pain points as comma-separated lists of pain-point numbers, and carrying reviewer challenges as threaded comments on the cell in question | Sequencing the board narrative: readiness gap, then the seven initiatives, then the three-step next-steps timeline, then firm qualifications and case studies | Post-workshop: a recap email restating five themes and six committed next steps, and warning that scoring will shift |

The pattern worth naming: Excel does arithmetic that a database should do, PowerPoint holds judgment that should be a first-class field, and the workshop produces the highest-value data in the engagement (client priority, urgency, dependencies, sizing, ownership) with no path back into the model except retyping.

### 2.4 Where the process leaks

| # | Failure mode | Evidence in the reference engagement | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Numeric scores stored as prose and recovered positionally | `=VALUE(LEFT(H7,1))` replicated across 43 rows x 3 dimensions in the master and 43 x 3 in the share copy; the visible cell holds the full anchor sentence | The score is a side effect of text formatting; a reworded rubric silently rescores the portfolio |
| 2 | Weights hard-coded into a formula row and duplicated | Weights appear in row 4 and again in row 5; `=SUMPRODUCT($I$5:$M$5,I7:M7)` reads only row 5 and spans two prose cells, relying on text-to-zero coercion | The weighting model cannot be changed safely or audited, and no record exists of what it was on any past date |
| 3 | Cross-workbook external references that break on copy | Theme resolution via `XLOOKUP(C7,'[1]Themes & Initiatives'!D:D, ...)`, the same pattern against `'[2]...'` in the hidden legacy sheet, and `SUMPRODUCT([1]Opportunities!$J$5:$N$5, ...)` for the operating-model weights | Neither workbook is self-contained; the intact taxonomy exists only in a hidden sheet of the client-facing copy |
| 4 | Taxonomy typed rather than enforced | The 18-row initiative picker list backs 17 initiatives because one name is duplicated unmerged; the same initiative appears as two names across sheets; some theme cells hold literal strings where others hold the lookup formula | Roll-ups by theme or initiative are wrong by an unknown amount, and no total can be trusted |
| 5 | Theme labels typo'd and drifting | One theme label carries a stray leading slash; another sheet spells a theme label with a transposed letter and combines two themes into a fifth name that appears nowhere else | The same theme reports different counts on different pages of the same deliverable |
| 6 | Three names for one horizon bucket | The quadrant formula emits "Sequence Later"; the recap email describes the same bucket as "Defer" in one sentence and "Future Horizon" in the next | The client cannot tell whether three frameworks or one is in play |
| 7 | An unreachable quadrant label | "Defend" requires business value below 3.5 and urgency at or above 3.5; across all 43 scored rows it is never produced, yet "Defend" is hand-typed once in a flattened copy sheet | A published framework has a category the arithmetic cannot generate, and a hand-typed exception that contradicts the formula |
| 8 | Formulas misaligned by one column from a given row down | From row 49 down, the Priority column holds `=SUM(M49+I49)/2` and the Business Value column holds `=K49`, one column left of the pattern in rows 7 to 48 | Rows past the boundary carry wrong priority bands with no visible error |
| 9 | A declared but never populated column | The master register declares "Span (L- Multi-year, M- Single Year, S-Quarter)" and leaves it empty for all 43 rows; the share copy populates it | Duration is asserted as an analytic dimension in the client-facing artifact and does not exist in the master |
| 10 | Discontiguous data-validation ranges | The foundational Yes/No dropdown is applied to `Y10 Y12:Y16 Y18:Y22 Y26:Y29 Y32:Y48`, leaving eight rows with no dropdown at all | Some opportunities cannot be marked foundational, which is exactly the field the recap email commits to populating |
| 11 | Free text in an enum cell | The Status column holds one of three short values on 25 rows and, on one row, a two-sentence question about whether a score should be a 5 | Status cannot be filtered or counted; an open analytic question is stored where a state belongs |
| 12 | Two incompatible status enums | In use: a three-value set. Declared, in a hidden sheet of the other workbook and never wired to any validation: a five-value review workflow. The maturity sheet's Status column uses three values from the second set | There is no single answer to "what is reviewed" for any record |
| 13 | Two ID schemes and two score scales | The live register has no ID column, so identity is Initiative text plus Opportunity text; a hidden sheet holds `OPP-01` to `OPP-27` on an 8 / 7 / 5 / 4 scale with its own effort grid; 27 and 43 do not reconcile | Two rankings of the same portfolio exist, both were shown to the client, and neither can be traced to the other |
| 14 | Conditional formatting keyed to retired labels | Four sheets carry cell-is rules testing four theme names that were renamed mid-engagement, plus duplicate rules for the same band differing only in letter case, plus a colour scale applied to a single stray cell | Colour on the page encodes a taxonomy that no longer exists, and colour is what executives read first |
| 15 | Enum column holding narrative prose | The hidden heat map declares an Investment Type legend of Defensive / Multiplier / Ceiling Remover, then fills that column with "so what" paragraphs | A declared classification dimension was never populated and cannot be recovered |
| 16 | Another client's material inside a live deliverable | The 33-slide working execution deck contains a 10-slide reusable-material section including a different client's platform estate and taxonomies | Confidentiality exposure created purely because the file, not the record, is the unit of work |
| 17 | Deck numbers drifting from the workbook | The deck states 4 themes, ~20 initiatives, ~50 opportunities and per-theme counts 13 / 16 / 19 / 8 summing to 56, against 17 initiatives and 43 + 12 rows in the workbooks; two slides carry a hand-typed "First draft" footer as the only staleness signal | The board-facing artifact and the analytical record disagree, and the only defence is a footnote |
| 18 | Duplicate focus-area names and a retained superseded register | One focus-area name appears twice under two different capability areas with different scores; a 55-row superseded register survives as a hidden sheet alongside the live 43-row one | Any count of focus areas or opportunities depends on which sheet the reader opened |

## 3. Users, Roles, and Jobs To Be Done

Nine roles. Consultant-side roles are drawn from the staffing pattern visible in the reference engagement's artifacts (a partner-level signer, a day-to-day lead who owned the final files, analysts who created and populated the workbooks, and reviewers challenging entries by comment thread). Client-side roles are drawn from the workshop attendee structure, the per-leader deep-dive slides, the sponsor goals-and-principles slides, and the board-narrative framing.

### 3.1 Consultant-side personas

**Engagement Partner / Lead (signing partner).** Needs a defensible chain from an executive-facing claim back to the evidence that supports it, and a way to see what changed since the last client conversation. Must never be able to alter a snapshot that has already been issued, or edit a canonical score without leaving a provenance record. Primary jobs: sign off the `Charter`; approve the `ScoringModel` before scoring begins; approve each phase gate; approve the board narrative and its exhibits; own the `Decision` log. Scope: read everything; write `Charter`, `ScoringModel` approval, phase-gate approvals, `Decision`, `NarrativeMessage`, `Deliverable` issuance.

**Engagement Manager.** Needs to keep 40-plus opportunities, 28 focus areas, and a workshop's worth of client input consistent while the taxonomy is still moving, and to know instantly what an edit breaks downstream. Must never be able to delete an `Evidence` or `AuditEvent` record, or bulk-accept `AISuggestion` records without individual review. Primary jobs: maintain the `Theme` / `Initiative` / `Opportunity` taxonomy; run the scoring and calibration pass; build `Wave` and `RoadmapScenario`; reconcile client-assigned priority rank against calculated score; assemble `Deliverable` sets; run the change-impact review before each client session. Scope: read/write everything within the engagement except `Charter` approval, phase-gate approval, and snapshot immutability.

**Analyst.** Needs to get interview transcripts, documents, and survey results into structured `Evidence`, `Finding`, and `Opportunity` records fast, with AI drafting and a human review step. Must never be able to publish a `Deliverable`, change a `ScoringModel`, or commit an `AISuggestion` that touches a scoring field (analyst may propose; manager or partner commits scores). Primary jobs: load `SourceDocument` and `Interview`; extract `Evidence` and `Finding`; draft `Opportunity` records and their recommended actions; maintain `MaturityFocusArea` evidence and rationale; build `CostLineItem` detail; prepare `Exhibit` drafts. Scope: read everything; write `SourceDocument`, `Interview`, `Evidence`, `Finding`, `Opportunity` drafts, `MaturityAssessment` drafts, `CostEstimate` detail, `Exhibit` drafts.

**Knowledge / Precedent Owner (firm-level, not engagement-level).** Needs to turn finished engagements into reusable, anonymized precedent that the AI can retrieve for cost ranges, rubric calibration, and initiative patterns, without ever exposing one client's material inside another client's workspace. This role exists specifically because the reference engagement's working deck carried another client's slides. Must never be able to read a live engagement's client-identifying fields, or push precedent directly into an engagement's canonical records (precedent enters only as an `AISuggestion`). Primary jobs: approve engagements for precedent release; run and verify anonymization; curate `Benchmark` and methodology templates; maintain rubric anchor libraries. Scope: read anonymized precedent library and methodology templates; write precedent library, `Benchmark`, methodology templates; no write access inside any live engagement.

### 3.2 Client-side personas

**CIO / CDIO (engagement sponsor).** Needs the assessment to be traceable to what their own leaders said, and their strategic goals and guiding principles to sit inside the model rather than on two orphan slides. Must never be able to change a score, a weight, a maturity level, or a snapshot. Primary jobs: review and challenge findings; record strategic goals and guiding principles as engagement inputs; register decisions and trade-offs; consume the sponsor view of the roadmap. Scope in MVP: read plus comment; `Decision` entries are captured by the consultant on their behalf.

**Functional Business Executive (EVP or VP owning a business domain).** Needs to see the roadmap filtered to their domain and understand what it costs them and what it buys them, which in the reference engagement was served by per-leader deep-dive slides. Must never be able to see other domains' cost detail or another executive's `StakeholderFeedback` attributed by name. Primary jobs: validate that findings in their domain are accurate; challenge sequencing that affects their commitments; supply value assumptions. Scope in MVP: read a domain-scoped projection, plus comment. **Read-only in MVP.**

**PMO / Transformation Office Lead.** Needs the roadmap to become trackable work: milestones, owners, dependencies, and a refresh cadence. This is the persona that the reference engagement had no artifact for at all. Must never be able to edit scores, weights, or the taxonomy, and must not be able to change the sequencing without a `Decision` record. Primary jobs: consume dependency and wave structure; report milestone and actuals status; flag slippage; request a refresh cycle. Scope in MVP: read plus comment; `Milestone` status and `ActualsSnapshot` are consultant-entered on their behalf. **Read-only in MVP** (see open question in §4.5).

**Board Member / CEO (narrative reader).** Needs a small number of defensible messages, each with the number behind it and the date it was true. Must never see draft or unreviewed content, or any figure not bound to an issued snapshot. Primary jobs: read the board narrative; see the investment and value trade-off; see the asks and decisions required. Scope in MVP: read the issued board `Deliverable` only, at a fixed snapshot. **Read-only in MVP.**

**Client Guest (generic external reviewer).** A named client participant with no domain scope, used for workshop participants who need the card set and the findings playback but nothing else. Scope in MVP: read a published workshop projection plus comment. **Read-only in MVP.**

### 3.3 Role-to-permission matrix

R = read, W = create/update, A = approve/commit, C = comment only, blank = no access. "AI commit" means authority to move an `AISuggestion` from `proposed` to `accepted` or `edited`.

| Capability | Partner / Lead | Manager | Analyst | Knowledge Owner | CIO / CDIO | Business Exec | PMO Lead | Board / CEO | Client Guest |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Create engagement, set phase gates | A | R | R |  | R |  |  |  |  |
| `Charter`, hypotheses, success criteria | A | W | R |  | C |  |  |  |  |
| `Stakeholder`, `Interview` plan | R | W | W |  | C |  |  |  |  |
| `SourceDocument`, `Evidence` | R | W | W |  | C | C | C |  | C |
| `Finding`, `Theme` narrative | A | W | W |  | C | C |  |  | C |
| `MaturityAssessment` levels and targets | A | W | W (draft) |  | C | C |  |  |  |
| `Opportunity` register and taxonomy | A | W | W (draft) |  | C | C |  |  | C |
| `ScoringModel` weights, bands, anchors | A | R | R | R (library) | R |  |  |  |  |
| `OpportunityScore` values | A | W | R |  | C | C |  |  | C |
| Client-assigned priority rank | A | W | W |  | C | C | C |  | C |
| `Dependency`, `Wave`, `RoadmapScenario` | A | W | R |  | C | C | C |  |  |
| `CostEstimate`, `ResourceDemand`, `CapacityProfile` | A | W | W (detail) |  | R | R (own domain) | R |  |  |
| `ValueCase`, `Benefit` | A | W | W (draft) |  | C | C |  | R |  |
| `Decision`, `StakeholderFeedback` | A | W | W |  | C | C | C |  | C |
| `NarrativeMessage`, `Exhibit` | A | W | W (draft) |  | C |  |  | R |  |
| Issue / re-issue `Deliverable` | A | R | R |  | R | R | R | R | R |
| `Milestone`, `KPI`, `ActualsSnapshot` | A | W | W |  | C | C | C |  |  |
| Commit an `AISuggestion` (non-scoring) | A | A | A |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| Commit an `AISuggestion` (scoring, weights, maturity level) | A | A |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| Comment threads on any entity | W | W | W | W | W | W | W |  | W |
| Read `AuditEvent` log | R | R | R | R |  |  |  |  |  |
| Precedent library (anonymized) | R | R | R | W |  |  |  |  |  |
| Release an engagement to precedent library | A | R |  | A |  |  |  |  |  |

Read-only in MVP: CIO / CDIO, Business Executive, PMO Lead, Board / CEO, Client Guest. All five may comment; none may write a canonical field. The Knowledge Owner is write-capable only outside live engagements.

## 4. Product Overview, Module Map, and Non-Goals

### 4.1 Modules

Nine modules, one per methodology phase plus ongoing activation. FR ranges are fixed here so the rest of the document lines up.

| Module | Name | One-line purpose | Phase | Primary entities | FR range |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | Charter & Mobilization | Turn a mandate into a scoped engagement with named stakeholders, an interview plan, a document request, and testable hypotheses | Week 0, Kickoff + Mobilization | `Engagement`, `Charter`, `Stakeholder`, `Interview` (planned), `SourceDocument` (requested) | FR-200 to FR-299 |
| M2 | Fact Base | Convert interviews, documents, surveys, and benchmarks into addressable evidence, findings, and an initiative inventory | Weeks 1 to 2, Interviews + Fact Gathering | `SourceDocument`, `Interview`, `Evidence`, `Finding`, `Benchmark`, `Theme` (emergent) | FR-300 to FR-399 |
| M3 | Maturity Assessment | Score 28 focus areas under 8 capability areas on a 5-level scale with current, target, and gap, each backed by evidence | Weeks 3 to 4, Current State Maturity | `CapabilityArea`, `MaturityFocusArea`, `MaturityAssessment`, `Evidence` | FR-400 to FR-499 |
| M4 | Opportunity Register, Scoring & Prioritization | Hold the enforced Theme to Initiative to Opportunity taxonomy and score every opportunity against a versioned weighted model | Weeks 3 to 4, Roadmap Prioritization Build | `Theme`, `Initiative`, `Opportunity`, `ScoreDimension`, `ScoringModel`, `OpportunityScore` | FR-500 to FR-599 |
| M5 | Roadmap Sequencing & Scenarios | Turn priority, dependencies, sizing, and business value into waves, scenarios, and a defensible V1 roadmap | Week 5, V1 Technology Roadmap | `Dependency`, `Wave`, `RoadmapScenario`, `RoadmapItem`, `Milestone` | FR-600 to FR-699 |
| M6 | Investment, Cost & Capacity Model | Pressure-test the roadmap against cost ranges, resource demand, and available capacity, and build the value case | Weeks 6 to 8, Investment, Cost + Capacity | `CostEstimate`, `CostLineItem`, `ResourceDemand`, `CapacityProfile`, `ValueCase`, `Benefit` | FR-700 to FR-799 |
| M7 | Business Alignment & Decision Log | Socialize the costed roadmap with business leaders, capture feedback and trade-offs as data, and record every decision | Weeks 9 to 10, Business Alignment + Refinement | `StakeholderFeedback`, `Decision`, `Risk`, `KPI`, `RoadmapScenario` (V2) | FR-800 to FR-899 |
| M8 | Narrative & Deliverable Generation | Generate the executive storyline, exhibits, board package, and 90-day activation plan from the model at a named snapshot | Weeks 10 to 12, Final Roadmap + Board Narrative | `NarrativeMessage`, `Exhibit`, `Deliverable`, `ActivationTask` | FR-900 to FR-999 |
| M9 | Living Roadmap & Activation | Keep the roadmap live: track milestones, actuals, benefits, and risks, detect slippage, and run refresh cycles | Ongoing, Roadmap Activation + Management | `Milestone`, `KPI`, `ActualsSnapshot`, `Risk`, `ActivationTask`, `RoadmapScenario` (refresh) | FR-1000 to FR-1099 |

Cross-cutting specifications:

| Concern | FR range |
|---|---|
| Platform, workspace, provenance, audit, versioning, comments, precedent library | FR-001 to FR-099 (this section) |
| Canonical data model and schemas | FR-100 to FR-199 |
| Calculation engine (derived fields, formula registry, recalculation) | FR-1100 to FR-1199 |
| Integrations and exports | FR-1200 to FR-1299 |
| Non-functional requirements | FR-1300 to FR-1399 |

### 4.2 Module map

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    M1["M1 Charter and Mobilization<br/>scope, stakeholders, hypotheses"] --> M2["M2 Fact Base<br/>evidence, findings, benchmarks"]
    M2 --> M3["M3 Maturity Assessment<br/>28 focus areas, current / target / gap"]
    M2 --> M4["M4 Opportunity Register and Scoring<br/>theme, initiative, opportunity, weighted score"]

    M7 --> M8["M8 Narrative and Deliverables<br/>messages, exhibits, board package"]
```
