The recommended MVP is the analytical spine of the engagement: fact base, maturity assessment, prioritized register, and a first-cut roadmap, on top of a real data model and a real calculation engine, with legacy workbook import and generated deck and workbook exports. That is where the reference engagement's analytical work actually sat, it is where every one of the known defects lived, and it is the smallest slice that a consultant can use end to end for a real engagement without falling back to Excel halfway through.

Cost and capacity modelling (M6), business alignment workflow (M7), and living-roadmap tracking (M9) are staged after, deliberately and explicitly. M6 is staged because the reference artifacts contained no cost model at all: the sequencing inputs slide named cost and resource constraints as inputs to "refine later", and no costed roadmap, capacity model or value case appears in the file set, so the product has no observed structure to build against and would be inventing one (see A-07). M7 is staged because it is a workflow product built on top of an artifact that must first exist and be trusted. M9 is staged because it only has value after a roadmap has been delivered, which by definition cannot happen in the MVP's own first engagement.

| Area | Feature | Status | Reason if not in MVP |
|---|---|---|---|

| Platform | Client-guest access and stakeholder views | v1.1 | Needed for M7 alignment, not for producing the artifact |
| Platform | Firm precedent library and anonymization pipeline | Later | Depends on a firm-level rights and process commitment (Q-07), not on engineering |
| Data model | All entities of §5, taxonomy with aliases, evidence and locators | In MVP | The spine |
| §7 Calculation engine | Scores, weighted score, bands, quadrants, rollups, maturity gaps, dependency validation | In MVP | Every defect being designed away is a calculation defect |

### 11.2 The MVP user journey, end to end

The walkthrough below is the single path the MVP must make smooth. Screen names are the ones defined in §6.

1. **Create the engagement.** In the `Engagement Setup wizard`, the lead names the client, selects the methodology template, sets phase dates against the 12-week calendar, and sets the confidentiality classification. In `Engagement Configuration` they confirm the `ScoringModel` (three dimensions, weights 0.40 / 0.35 / 0.25, 1-to-5 anchored scale), the band thresholds (4.5 / 3.75 / 2.8), the quadrant definition and threshold (3.5), the horizon labels, the t-shirt scale, and the maturity framework (CMMI-style, 5 levels). *No AI.*
2. **Optionally carry in an existing engagement.** In the `Legacy Import Wizard` the consultant drops in prior workbooks, assigns sheet roles, confirms header and weight rows, maps columns, works the `ValidationReport` to zero blockers, and promotes. The register, taxonomy and maturity assessment now exist with every defect resolved and recorded. *No AI, deliberately: the importer is deterministic.*
3. **Set up the fact base.** In `Stakeholder Map` and `Document Request List` the team records who they will speak to and what they have asked for. *AI-01 reads the initial document set, summarizes it, and lists what is missing against the methodology's expected input types.*
4. **Ingest sources.** Documents and transcripts land in the `Ingest queue`. *AI-05 extracts structured records per FR-1230 (strategic objectives, applications, in-flight initiatives, org roles, constraints). AI-04 synthesizes each transcript into candidate findings with speaker attribution and transcript locators.* The consultant reviews every extraction in the `Interview workspace` and `Evidence repository`.
5. **Shape the findings.** In the `Finding register` the consultant merges, splits and promotes. *AI-06 clusters findings into candidate themes with a stated cluster rationale.* The consultant reshapes clusters on the `Theme board` and promotes the canonical `Theme` set that M4 will use.
6. **Assess maturity.** In the `Assessment grid` the consultant works through the focus areas. *AI-09 proposes a current level per focus area with the evidence it relied on and an explicit statement of what would move the level up. AI-10 proposes root causes behind each gap.* The consultant sets current and target levels; gap and label compute. The `Heatmap` is now a live view, not a drawn slide.
7. **Generate the opportunity candidates.** From `Gap-to-opportunity`, *AI-11 proposes opportunities from the gaps*, each carrying the gap and the evidence it came from. The consultant accepts into the register, edits titles and recommended actions, and writes the "so what".
8. **Clean the register.** *AI-12 proposes duplicate and near-duplicate pairs* on the `Duplicates` screen with a side-by-side diff. The consultant merges, keeps both with a stated distinction, or rejects.
9. **Score.** In `Bulk scoring and triage` the consultant scores each opportunity on the three dimensions against the anchored scale. *AI-13 proposes a score per dimension with cited evidence and the anchor it matched.* The consultant accepts, edits, or overrides. Weighted score, band, quadrant axes and quadrant label compute on every keystroke. The `Calibration` view shows the distribution so a scorer drifting high is visible.
10. **Read the prioritization.** The `Quadrant 2x2` and `Bubble chart` render from the live model. *AI-17 narrates why a given opportunity outranks another, citing the dimension deltas and the evidence.* The consultant uses that narration as the seed of the rationale text.
11. **Bring in the room's view.** After the workshop, the consultant imports the board output (FR-1251). `clientRank`, `clientUrgency` and `clientEffort` land as attributed fields. The `Reconciliation` screen lists every divergence between the room's ranking and the calculated band, and the consultant resolves each into a `Decision` or an accepted divergence.
12. **Build the dependency picture.** *AI-14 proposes typed dependencies between initiatives from the architecture and finding evidence.* The consultant confirms or rejects each on the `Dependency Graph`. *AI-16 explains every dependency conflict and infeasibility* on the `Feasibility Panel`, and the consultant resolves them.
13. **Sequence the first-cut roadmap.** In the `Wave Designer` and `Roadmap Gantt` the consultant assigns initiatives to waves and workstreams, sets owners and target outcomes, and reads the feasibility flags. The `Rationale Card` per initiative captures why it sits where it sits.
14. **Compare an alternative.** In `Scenario Manager` the consultant clones the scenario, moves a wave, and diffs. The diff names what moved, what broke, and what was unblocked.
15. **Check integrity before issuing.** The `Validation Center` lists every unresolved validation error, every number with no basis, every stale narrative binding, and every taxonomy violation. *AI-30 reports staleness and internal inconsistency across the deliverable set.* Target state is zero on each.
16. **Build and issue the deliverables.** In the `Deliverable Builder` the consultant selects the template and the slide set, and every figure binds to the snapshot. `Export Center` runs the confidentiality scan, takes the `ModelSnapshot`, and produces the deck, the client-shareable workbook, the PDF and the recap narrative, each stamped with the snapshot reference. The escape-hatch download is offered and recorded.

```mermaid

  A["Engagement Setup wizard<br/>+ Engagement Configuration"] --> B{"Existing workbook<br/>to carry in?"}
  B -->|yes| C["Legacy Import Wizard<br/>roles, mapping, ValidationReport to zero"]
  B -->|no| D["Stakeholder Map<br/>+ Document Request List<br/>AI-01"]

  D --> E["Ingest queue<br/>AI-04 transcripts, AI-05 documents"]
```

### 11.3 Build sequence

The stages below are ordered so that the data model and the calculation engine land before any AI capability. That ordering is not a preference, and it has four concrete justifications.

First, every AI capability in this product is a proposal against a typed field. AI-13 proposes a score on a 1-to-5 anchored scale for a named dimension; AI-09 proposes a maturity level within a framework; AI-14 proposes a typed dependency between two `Initiative` records. None of those has a target to write into until the schema exists, and building them against a moving schema is rework with extra steps.

Second, the value of an accepted proposal is entirely in what happens next: accepting a score must recompute the weighted score, the band, the quadrant, the initiative rollup, the theme rollup and the roadmap feasibility flags, and must be auditable back to the evidence. Without the engine, accepting a suggestion writes a number into a box, which is what the spreadsheet already does.

Third, the defects this product exists to remove are calculation and schema defects, not AI defects. A first-character score extraction, a hard-coded weight, a formula that stops matching its column, a lookup through a broken external reference, and an enum with gaps are all failures of the deterministic layer. Shipping AI on top of an unreliable engine produces confident proposals feeding wrong arithmetic, which is worse than the spreadsheet.

Fourth, there is no way to evaluate an AI capability without a deterministic baseline. Measuring whether AI-13's proposal changed the answer requires an answer that is stable and reproducible, which is exactly what the engine plus snapshots provide.

| Stage | Delivers | Depends on | Demonstrable proof it works |
|---|---|---|---|
| S0 Foundations | Engagement lifecycle, roles, per-engagement scoped data access, append-only audit log, content-addressed snapshots, entity CRUD scaffolding | Nothing | The isolation test suite of AC-1300.1 to AC-1300.3 passes; an entity's full history replays to its current state (AC-1330.3) |
| S1 Data model and taxonomy | All §5 entities, `Theme` to `Initiative` to `Opportunity` hierarchy with aliases, `ScoringModel` as data with versioned weights, anchors and thresholds, enum enforcement | S0 | The reference engagement's 4 themes, 17 initiatives and 55 opportunities exist as records with no name collision, and a theme rename does not orphan a row |
| S2 Calculation engine | §7 engine: per-dimension scores, weighted score, band, quadrant axes and label, rollups, maturity gap and label, dependency validity, with a full dependency graph and incremental recompute | S1 | The engine reproduces every cached value in the reference workbooks to the cent for every row that was not affected by a known defect, and names the defect for every row where it does not (AC-1204.1). A weight change recomputes 500 rows inside FR-1342 |
| S3 Register and maturity UI | `Register tree`, `Opportunity detail`, `Bulk scoring and triage`, `Scoring guide`, `Calibration`, `Quadrant 2x2`, `Bubble chart`, `Assessment grid`, `Focus area detail`, `Heatmap` | S2 | A consultant scores 55 opportunities and 28 focus areas end to end with keyboard only, faster than in the workbook, meeting AC-1341.2 |
| S4 Legacy import | §9.1 in full: role detection, mapping, the eight defect classes, validation report, transform log, manifest, rollback | S1, S2, S3 | Both reference workbooks import to zero blockers, and the validation report independently discovers every one of the eight known defects without being told they are there |
| S5 Ingestion and evidence | Document extraction, transcript ingestion, speaker attribution, transcript locators, `Evidence repository`, `Finding register` | S1 | A finding opens its source at the exact span; a re-transcription does not break an existing citation (AC-1222.1) |
| S6 AI suggestion framework | The generic `AISuggestion` lifecycle: proposal, evidence citation, confidence, accept, accept-with-edit, reject-with-reason, abstain, full logging per FR-1370, latency classes per FR-1344 | S2, S5 | A stub capability round-trips through accept, edit, reject and abstain, and every §12.3 metric computes from the logs alone |
| S7 AI capabilities, spine | AI-05, AI-04, AI-01, AI-06, AI-09, AI-10, AI-11, AI-12, AI-13, AI-17 | S6 | Each capability's evaluation-harness run meets its §12.3 targets on a held-out set; every proposal carries a resolvable locator |
| S8 Sequencing and scenarios | `Sequencing Inputs board`, `Dependency Graph`, `Feasibility Panel`, `Wave Designer`, `Roadmap Gantt`, `Scenario Manager` and diff, plus AI-14 and AI-16 | S2, S7 | A dependency cycle is detected and explained; a scenario diff over target scale meets FR-1343; a first-cut roadmap for the reference register is produced and sequenced |
| S9 Exports and snapshots | Deck template binding, exhibit catalogue with native-chart rendering, PowerPoint, Excel, PDF and narrative exports, export manifest, byte-identical regeneration | S2, S3, S8 | Regenerating 20 stored deliverables yields identical hashes (AC-1332.1); every native chart's embedded worksheet equals the snapshot (AC-1262.2) |
| S10 Integrity and confidentiality | `Validation Center`, AI-30, export confidentiality scan, FR-1313 SPOF rule, redaction operation, classification enforcement, integrity canary | S9 | A deck containing another engagement's exhibit is blocked; a named individual redacts across the engagement in under 60 seconds with zero residual hits; the canary detects an injected divergence |
| S11 Whiteboard import and reconciliation | FR-1251 board import, `clientRank` capture, `Reconciliation` screen | S3, S4 | A board export lands as attributed fields with no retyping, and every divergence appears as a resolvable line |
| S12 Hardening and pilot readiness | Performance to the FR-134x budgets at target scale, backup and restore drill, accessibility pass, observability dashboards, escape hatch | All | A loaded target-scale engagement meets every latency budget; a restore drill regenerates a deliverable byte-identically (AC-1351.1) |

### 11.4 The demo-scale slice

The smallest thing that credibly proves the concept is a five-minute demonstration built on stages S0 through S4 plus two AI capabilities from S7. It proves the thesis, which is not "AI writes your roadmap" but "the analytical spine becomes a live model instead of a spreadsheet, and the numbers stop drifting".

**Screens required:** `Legacy Import Wizard`, `Register tree`, `Opportunity detail`, `Bulk scoring and triage`, `Engagement Configuration`, `Quadrant 2x2`, and a single-template `Export Center`.

**AI capabilities required:** AI-13 (score proposal per dimension with cited evidence), AI-17 (prioritization rationale narration), and, if time allows, AI-12 (duplicate consolidation). Nothing else. Extraction and clustering are more impressive in the abstract and far less convincing in a demo, because they take minutes to run and their output is hard to judge in a room.

**What the demonstrator shows, in sequence:**

1. Drop the anonymized copies of two real prior engagement workbooks into the importer. Show the sheet-role list, including the hidden sheets, and the detected header and weight rows.
2. Open the `ValidationReport`. Walk three lines out loud: the score column that is prose with the numeral extracted by a first-character read, the row from which the priority-band column stopped holding the band formula, and the theme-name cluster with five members where the file's own taxonomy has four. Resolve each in a click. This is the moment the audience recognizes their own files.
3. Promote the import. The register appears with scores as integers, anchors as labels, rationale as prose, one canonical taxonomy, and a maturity grid whose gaps compute.
4. In `Engagement Configuration`, change the Financial Impact weight from 0.40 to 0.50. Show the band movement summary appearing inside two seconds: the count of rows that changed band, and which ones. State plainly that in the source workbook this weight was typed inside a formula in one cell of one row and could not be changed or tested at all.
5. Open an unscored opportunity in `Opportunity detail` and invoke AI-13. Show the proposed score per dimension, the anchor it matched, and the two or three pieces of cited evidence with clickable locators into the interview transcript and the strategy document. Accept one, edit one down a level with a reason, reject one. Show the register recompute.
6. In `Quadrant 2x2`, click the highest-ranked opportunity and invoke AI-17. Read the narration: why this outranks the next one, in dimension deltas and evidence, in language a consultant would use in front of a client.
7. Export the one-page register exhibit and the client-shareable workbook. Open the workbook: no hidden sheets, no external references, scores as integers in their own columns, a `Method` sheet stating the weights and thresholds actually applied, and a snapshot reference. Open the exported exhibit and show that its embedded data equals the register.
8. Close on the one sentence that matters: the deck, the workbook and the model cannot disagree, because there is only one of them.

### 11.5 Risks to delivery

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Consultants do not trust AI-proposed scores, so the register is hand-typed anyway and the product is a slower spreadsheet | High | High. It removes the product's main efficiency claim and leaves only the integrity claim | Never present a proposal without its cited evidence and the anchor it matched (A-08). Make the proposal a starting point in an editable field, never a committed value. Track blind-accept rate and edit magnitude, not just acceptance (§12.3), and treat a low proposal-view rate as a product defect rather than user error. Ship the deterministic value first: even with every proposal rejected, the product still beats the workbook on recompute, taxonomy integrity and export fidelity, so adoption does not depend on trust arriving early |
| The product's structure fights how a consultant actually thinks mid-engagement, so it gets abandoned in week three for a spreadsheet | High | High. The reference evidence shows consultants working fast and messily: renaming themes mid-engagement, leaving a column declared and empty, keeping an old register in a hidden sheet, arguing about whether an opportunity belongs in one bucket or another in threaded comments | Support the messy states as first-class rather than forbidding them: a `Draft` opportunity with no scores, a `Candidate` theme not yet in the taxonomy, a rename that carries aliases forward, a superseded row that stays visible with its history, and a threaded comment on any field. Never block a save on completeness; block only issuing a deliverable. Pilot with one live engagement in parallel with its spreadsheet and instrument where the consultant leaves the product |
| Legacy import proves harder than expected because real files are more varied than the two examined | Medium | High. Import is the adoption precondition | Build the importer as a mapping-and-report engine rather than a parser for one shape, so an unrecognized structure degrades to more decisions rather than to failure. Collect five to eight further historical workbooks before S4 starts and test against all of them. Treat "the report found a defect class we had not enumerated" as the expected outcome and make the defect catalogue extensible |
| The firm never commits to the anonymized precedent library, so AI-08 and AI-18 never ship and cost estimation stays manual | Medium | Medium. It removes the precedent-based cost range, which is a differentiator but not the spine | Keep the `PrecedentSource` interface (FR-1291) as the only coupling, so nothing else depends on the library's existence. Sequence AI-08 and AI-18 to Later. Escalate Q-07 as a firm-leadership decision early, since it is a rights and process question, not an engineering one |
| The three-dimension scoring model turns out to be one engagement's choice rather than the firm's standard | Medium | Medium to high, depending on how different other engagements are | Hold the `ScoringModel` as versioned data from S1, never as code: dimension count, names, weights, scale, anchors and band thresholds are all configuration. Validate against three further engagements' workbooks during S1 (A-02) |
| Deck fidelity is not good enough, so consultants export and then rebuild slides by hand | Medium | High. It reintroduces the drift the product exists to prevent | Bind to named layouts and placeholders, not positions (FR-1260). Detect text overflow at render time (AC-1261.3). Measure the hand-edit rate after export as an explicit success metric (§12.5 C5) and treat above 10% as a product defect |
| Scope creep into cost modelling because a client asks for it mid-pilot | Medium | Medium. M6 without an estimating basis produces invented numbers presented with product authority | Hold the line stated in 11.1: no `CostEstimate` in the MVP, and the product shows cost fields as explicitly absent rather than empty. Resolve A-07 by asking for the firm's actual estimating basis before building M6 |
| Performance degrades at real scale because the calculation graph is recomputed naively | Medium | Medium. A register that takes four seconds to respond to a score entry is slower than Excel and will lose | Build incremental recomputation over an explicit dependency graph in S2, not as an S12 optimization. Load-test at target scale from S3 onward, not at the end |
| A confidentiality incident during the pilot (a client-facing artifact carrying named individuals, another client's content, or security detail) | Low, but the reference artifacts show the pattern is normal | Severe. It is an existential risk to the firm's client relationships and to the product | Ship the export scan, the SPOF rule and cross-client blocking in S10 before any client-facing export leaves the product, not as hardening. Make blocks blocks, not warnings. Treat any incident as a P1 with a mandatory report |
| Byte-identical regeneration proves impractical against a chosen rendering library | Low to medium | Medium. It undermines the reproducibility claim in FR-1332 | Prove regeneration on a trivial deck in S9's first week, before the exhibit catalogue is built. If the library cannot be made deterministic, that is a library-selection decision, and it must be made early |

## 12. Success Metrics and Evaluation

### 12.1 Engagement-efficiency metrics

An honesty statement first, because it governs how every number in this sub-section should be read. No time was measured in the reference engagement. What is observable is artifact structure and file metadata: the shape and row counts of two workbooks and four decks, the dates on a recap and on a planning deck, and the creation and last-modified timestamps on the workbooks. From those, elapsed intervals can be derived and effort can only be inferred. Specifically: the two assessment workbooks' creation timestamps are 37 days apart; the master assessment workbook was created on the first day of the two-day onsite; both workbooks were still being modified 41 days after the onsite closed; and the final planning deck is dated approximately 12 weeks after the onsite. The baselines below are therefore inferred from structure and interval, not from measured consultant time, and the targets are directional until the first three engagements on the product are instrumented.

| Metric | How measured | Inferred baseline | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Elapsed days, first source ingested to first exported prioritized register | Product timestamps: earliest source upload to first register export | 37 days between the two reference workbooks' creation, with the master created on the workshop's first day | ≤ 15 days |
| Elapsed days, workshop close to a stable scored register | Product timestamps: workshop import to the last score edit before deliverable issue | 41 days of continued workbook editing after the onsite closed | ≤ 10 days |
| Elapsed days, kickoff to first-cut roadmap deck issued | Engagement start to first issued roadmap `Deliverable` | The reference reached an execution-planning deck approximately 12 weeks after the onsite | ≤ 6 weeks from kickoff |
| Deliverable slides generated versus hand-authored | Count of slides bound to a snapshot over total slides in issued decks | 0 of roughly 130 slides across four decks were generated; all were hand-built | ≥ 70% generated in MVP, ≥ 85% by v1.1 |
| Time from a scoring or sequencing change to a refreshed deliverable | Product timing: model change to completed export | Manual, unmeasured, and demonstrably long enough that a recap email had to warn recipients the deck's rankings would shift | ≤ 5 minutes, unattended |
| Hand-transcription steps between tools per engagement | Count of instances where a value is retyped from one artifact into another, recorded during pilot observation | At least three observable: workshop board into a register column, register into deck exhibits, register into the derived share copy | 0 |
| Duplicate maintenance of the same dataset | Count of artifacts holding the same register independently | 2 workbooks holding overlapping registers plus a superseded hidden sheet plus an older register sheet | 1 |
| Consultant hours per issued deliverable | Time tracking, pilot only | No baseline exists. This must be instrumented from the first pilot engagement, and no target should be claimed before it is | Establish baseline, then reduce 30% |
| Rework after a late input | Count of edits to issued deliverables within 14 days of issue | Unmeasurable from the artifacts, though the recap's own caveat implies it was substantial | Reduce; establish baseline in pilot |

### 12.2 Quality and integrity metrics

These are the metrics that justify the product's existence independently of any efficiency claim. Every one of them corresponds to a defect that was actually present in the reference artifacts, and every one is mechanically preventable. Five of them target exactly zero, and zero is the correct target rather than an aspiration: for each of the five, the product either blocks the issue or the metric registering above zero is a bug in the product, not a lapse by the consultant.

| Metric | Definition | Target | Why this target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unresolved validation errors at deliverable issue | Count of open `Blocker` and undecided `Decision` lines on any engagement at the moment a `Deliverable` is marked issued | **0** | The `Validation Center` blocks issue. Any non-zero value means a bypass exists |
| Numbers in an issued deliverable with no basis | Count of figures in an issued artifact that do not resolve to a snapshot binding | **0** | FR-1261 permits no path for a typed number. Non-zero means a binding failed silently |
| Stale narrative bindings at export | Count of bound values in an issued artifact whose source changed after the narrative was authored and before the snapshot | **0** | AI-30 detects it and the scan blocks it. This is the deck-drifts-from-workbook defect, made impossible |
| Foreign-client content in an issued deliverable | Count of exhibits, narrative blocks or slides whose provenance is another engagement | **0** | Observed in the reference file set. FR-1264 blocks it |
| External or cross-file references in an exported workbook | Count of formulas referencing another file | **0** | FR-1272 forbids formulas of this kind entirely |
| Taxonomy violations | Count of theme or initiative strings on live records that are not canonical taxonomy members, plus orphan initiatives, plus aliases used as canonical labels | 0 on issue; ≤ 5 open at any time mid-engagement | Mid-engagement candidates are legitimate. Shipping one is not |
| Broken evidence locators | Count of `Evidence` records whose locator no longer resolves | 0 | AC-1222.2 makes it visible rather than silent |
| Scored opportunities with no evidence citation | Share of scored opportunities with zero `Evidence` on any dimension | ≤ 5% overall; **0** for bands Critical and High | A Critical-band judgment with no cited evidence is the one thing a client will challenge |
| Duplicate pairs surviving to issue | Share of issued opportunities that AI-12 flags as a duplicate pair at confidence above 0.8 and that were never adjudicated | ≤ 2% | Observed in the reference register, where reviewer comments questioned whether two opportunities were the same thing and the question was never closed in the data |
| Stored-versus-recomputed divergence | Count of derived values whose stored value differs from a fresh recomputation, from the FR-1354 canary | **0** | This is the reference workbook's core failure mode. It should be structurally impossible, and the canary exists to prove it |
| Enum integrity | Count of enum-typed fields holding a value outside their enum, or with partial validation coverage | 0 | Observed in the reference workbooks as prose in an enum column and a validation range with gaps |

### 12.3 AI quality metrics by capability class

| Class | Capabilities | Acceptance unchanged | Edit rate | Median edit magnitude | Abstention | Evidence citation compliance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Extraction | AI-01, AI-04, AI-05 | 55 to 75% | 20 to 40% | ≤ 15% of field content changed | 5 to 15% | 100%. An extracted value with no locator is a defect, not a low-confidence result |
| Clustering and consolidation | AI-06, AI-12 | 40 to 65% of proposed clusters or pairs accepted as proposed | 25 to 45% reshaped | ≤ 30% of membership changed | 10 to 20% | 100% of cluster members traceable to their source records |
| Judgment proposal | AI-09, AI-13, AI-14 | 50 to 70% | 25 to 45% | ≤ 1 level or 1 score point | 10 to 25% | ≥ 95% of proposals carry at least one resolvable locator; 100% for proposals at the top two levels |
| Analysis and detection | AI-07, AI-10, AI-16, AI-19, AI-30, AI-31, AI-32 | 60 to 80% of flags confirmed as real | n/a | n/a | n/a. Instead: false-positive rate ≤ 25%, and recall against a seeded defect set ≥ 90% | 100% of flags name the records involved |
| Generation | AI-17, AI-22, AI-25, AI-26, AI-27, AI-29, AI-34 | 25 to 45% | 55 to 75% | ≤ 40% of text changed | 5 to 10% | 100% of quantitative assertions bound to a snapshot value; ≥ 90% of qualitative assertions carry an evidence link |
| Retrieval-grounded estimation | AI-08, AI-18 | 35 to 60% | 30 to 55% | ≤ 25% of the range width | 20 to 35% | 100% of ranges state the contributing precedent count and the basis year |

Additional metrics tracked for every class: time-to-decision; blind-accept rate (accepted in under 3 seconds without the evidence panel being opened), target < 10%; proposal-view rate (share of proposals a consultant actually looked at), target > 70%, because a low value means the feature is being ignored rather than trusted; and rejection-reason distribution, because a rising `not_evidenced` share is a retrieval problem while a rising `miscalibrated` share is a prompt or anchor problem.

**What a too-high acceptance rate would indicate.** For a generation capability, high acceptance is a reasonable signal. For a judgment capability such as AI-13, an acceptance-unchanged rate above roughly 85% is a warning, not a win, and it means one of three things. First, the consultant may be rubber-stamping, which shows as acceptance near 100% alongside an edit rate near zero, a time-to-decision of a couple of seconds, and a blind-accept rate above 10%. That is worse than no capability at all, because it launders a machine guess into a client-facing judgment while wearing the authority of consultant review. Second, the capability may be proposing only the easy cases and abstaining on everything genuinely uncertain, which shows as high acceptance alongside a high abstention rate. Third, and most insidious, the capability may be proposing the centre of the scale everywhere: a capability that answers 3 on every dimension will look agreeable, will move nothing, and will produce a register in which nothing is prioritized. That shows as high acceptance alongside a proposal distribution with much lower variance than the consultants' own final distribution.

Acceptance is therefore never read alone. It is read against edit magnitude, abstention rate, time-to-decision, blind-accept rate, and the variance and shape of the proposal distribution compared with the final human distribution, all of which the `Calibration` view and the AI capability health dashboard show side by side.

### 12.4 Client and adoption metrics

| Metric | How measured | Target | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stakeholder-view reach | Share of named stakeholders with a `StakeholderView` who opened it at least once before the aligned roadmap is issued | ≥ 60% | Ships with v1.1 client access. The reference engagement's equivalent was a slide deck emailed to roughly 21 client recipients with no way to know who read it |
| Stakeholder-view depth | Median distinct sessions per stakeholder over the alignment phase | ≥ 2 | One visit is compliance; two is use |
| Structured decisions logged per engagement | Count of `Decision` records with date, owner, options considered and rationale | ≥ 20 | Baseline unknown: the reference engagement produced a decision log as a deck section, with no structured record and therefore no count |
| Feedback captured in-product | Share of stakeholder feedback items entering as structured feedback rather than by email or a marked-up deck | ≥ 70% | The reference path was reply-all email and threaded workbook comments |
| Divergences resolved | Share of client-rank versus calculated-band divergences closed with a `Decision` or an explicit accepted-divergence note before issue | 100% | The reference engagement carried these unresolved, and warned about it in writing |
| Roadmap still being updated at 90 days | Share of delivered engagements with at least one model edit between day 60 and day 90 after final issue | ≥ 50% | This is the single test of whether "living roadmap" is real or is a slide title |
| Refresh cycles completed | Count of governance refresh cycles completed in the first 90 days after issue | ≥ 1 per engagement | Requires M9; measured from v1.2 |
| Client-guest weekly actives during alignment | Distinct guest users per week in the alignment phase | ≥ 5 | A proxy for whether clients will accept a browser tool at all (A-05) |
| Consultant weekly actives | Distinct consultants using the product in a delivery week per active engagement | ≥ 80% of the assigned team | A team member who never opens it is producing content somewhere else |

### 12.5 Definition of MVP success

MVP success is defined as six falsifiable claims. Each has a measurement that would confirm it and a stated condition that would refute it. If three or more are refuted, the MVP has not succeeded regardless of how the rest look.

**C1. A consultant can carry an existing engagement workbook into the product and get a correct live register, in under one working day, without retyping.**
Confirmed if: for each of three real historical workbook sets, the import reaches zero `Blocker` and zero undecided `Decision` lines within 8 tracked working hours, and the recomputed weighted score matches the source's cached value for at least 95% of rows, with every mismatch attributed by the report to a named defect class.
Refuted if: any set requires more than two working days, or more than 5% of rows show unexplained divergence, or a consultant retypes any row.

**C2. The product's numbers and its deliverables cannot disagree.**
Confirmed if: across every deliverable issued during the pilot, the count of figures with no snapshot binding is zero, the count of stale bindings at issue is zero, and every issued deliverable regenerates byte-identically from its snapshot.
Refuted if: any issued deliverable contains a figure the product cannot trace, or any regeneration produces a different artifact.

**C3. Consultants use AI proposals as a genuine starting point rather than ignoring or rubber-stamping them.**
Confirmed if, for AI-13 across the pilot: proposal-view rate above 70%, acceptance-unchanged plus light-edit between 50% and 85%, blind-accept rate below 10%, and at least 80% of scored opportunities have an AI proposal somewhere in their score history.
Refuted if: proposal-view rate is below 30% (ignored), or acceptance-unchanged exceeds 90% with a median edit magnitude of zero and a proposal distribution materially flatter than the human distribution (rubber-stamped).

**C4. The prioritized register plus first-cut roadmap is produced faster than the spreadsheet path.**
Confirmed if: instrumented elapsed time from first source upload to first issued roadmap deliverable is at most half the reference engagement's inferred equivalent interval, on at least two of three pilot engagements.
Refuted if: elapsed time equals or exceeds the reference interval on two or more pilots, or if the consultant maintains a parallel spreadsheet through to delivery.

**C5. A product-generated client-facing artifact is accepted for an executive audience without being rebuilt by hand.**
Confirmed if: for each pilot engagement, the issued deck was exported from the product and fewer than 10% of its slides were edited outside the product after export, measured by comparing the exported file against the file actually presented.
Refuted if: consultants export and then rebuild, or if the presented file differs from the exported file on more than 25% of slides.

**C6. The product does not leak.**
Confirmed if: zero cross-engagement content incidents; zero individuals named as a single point of failure in an issued client artifact without a recorded FR-1313 confirmation; zero `Restricted` content in a client-external artifact; and a completed confidentiality scan record on 100% of issued deliverables.
Refuted if: any one of those counts is non-zero. This claim has no tolerance, because a single incident of any of them is a client-relationship event for the firm.

## 13. Assumptions

Each assumption below states what is assumed, why the assumption was necessary to write this PRD, what the risk is if it is wrong, and how it could be validated cheaply. "Cheaply" means without building anything.

| ID | Assumption | Why it was necessary | Risk if wrong | Cheap validation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A-01 | The reference engagement is representative of how the firm runs a transformation roadmap engagement, in method, depth and output shape | It is the only engagement observed. Every inference about what consultants analyse, what structures they create, and what defects recur derives from it | The product optimizes for one engagement's habits. Modules could be structurally wrong: the wrong entity as the unit of prioritization, the wrong deliverable set, the wrong phase boundaries | Have three other engagement leads walk through their own most recent file set against §2's as-is description and mark what differs. Two hours each |
| A-02 | The three-dimension weighted scoring model (Financial Impact 0.40, Risk if Deferred 0.35, Strategic Alignment 0.25, anchored 1 to 5) is the firm's standard method, not one engagement's invention | The whole of M4 and §7 is built on it, and the register, quadrant and roadmap sequencing all consume it | If it is per-engagement, the `ScoringModel` must be far more configurable than assumed, and firm-level calibration, precedent-based cost bands and cross-engagement comparison all become meaningless | Collect the scoring sheet from three other engagements and compare dimensions, weights, scale and anchor text. One hour. This also answers Q-01 |
| A-03 | A CMMI-style five-level model is the default maturity framework, with other frameworks available as alternatives | M3 needs a default, and the reference used a CMMI v2.0 framework with an informal appraisal method, calibrated against a named analyst maturity descriptor set | If the firm routinely uses several frameworks with different level counts and semantics, the framework registry must be a first-class configuration surface in the MVP rather than a v1.1 nicety | Ask the assessment leads which frameworks they have used in the last eight engagements and with how many levels. One conversation |
| A-04 | An engagement is single-client, single-currency and single-language in the MVP, with logical rather than cryptographic isolation between engagements in a single firm tenant | It removes multi-entity consolidation, FX handling, translation and per-tenant key management from scope, all of which would otherwise touch the data model and every calculation | A multi-country client needing per-region currency, or a client demanding a dedicated encryption key or a dedicated tenant, cannot be served. Currency in particular is hard to retrofit into a cost model | Check the firm's last two years of engagement list for multi-currency clients, and check whether any client contract already requires customer-managed keys. One afternoon with the commercial team |
| A-05 | Clients will accept and use a browser-based roadmap tool, in addition to (not instead of) a deck | M7 and M9 depend on client users logging in. The MVP does not, which is why it is only an assumption for the staged modules | If clients refuse to log in, the product is a consultant-side tool only. The living-roadmap thesis and the stakeholder-view feature both collapse, and §12.4 becomes unmeasurable | Ask two recent client sponsors directly whether they would open a link weekly. Also observable: whether the interactive roadmap tool named in the methodology's final phase was ever actually delivered and used on a prior engagement |
| A-06 | The firm can build an anonymized precedent library and has the contractual rights to derive anonymized records from past client engagements | AI-08 and AI-18, and any cross-engagement cost band or benchmark, depend on it entirely | Precedent-based cost estimation never exists. AI-18 must be replaced with a manually maintained internal estimating basis, and the firm's main claimed advantage over a generic tool is unavailable | Have counsel review two representative client MSAs for a work-product and anonymized-derivative clause. One review. This is Q-07 |
| A-07 | Detailed cost, capacity and value modelling was performed on the reference engagement outside the artifacts examined, rather than not performed at all | The methodology's Weeks 6 to 8 phase specifies a costed roadmap, capacity requirements, initiative-level cost ranges and a value case, and none of it appears in the file set. The onsite deck explicitly listed cost and resource constraints as inputs to "refine later" | If it was never done in that structured form, M6 has no observed basis and would be entirely invented: cost categories, estimating method, capacity model and value framework would all be product opinions presented with product authority | Ask for the cost model from any engagement that reached the investment phase. If none exists, that is itself the answer, and M6 must start from the firm's estimating standards rather than from an artifact |
| A-08 | Consultants will accept an AI proposal only when the evidence behind it is visible and clickable, and will reject or ignore proposals presented as bare assertions | It drives the evidence-citation requirement on every capability, the 100% citation targets in §12.3, and the design of every proposal surface | If consultants do not care about evidence, the citation machinery is expensive and unused. More dangerously, if they accept without it, §12.5 C3's rubber-stamping failure becomes the normal case and the product launders guesses | Show three consultants two mock proposals for the same score, one with citations and one without, and ask which they would accept and what they would do next. Thirty minutes |
| A-09 | The `Opportunity` is the unit of prioritization and scoring, with `Initiative` as a grouping above it and `Theme` above that | The register, the scoring model, the quadrant and the roadmap all assume it. The reference workbook scored at opportunity level and rolled up | If the firm sometimes scores at initiative level, rollup direction reverses and the roadmap sequences a different object than the one that carries the score | Check whether any other engagement's register scores at initiative level. One hour |
| A-10 | Operating-model opportunities are the same kind of object as technology opportunities and belong in the same register | §5 has one `Opportunity` entity. The reference kept them in a separate sheet with the same column structure, the same three dimensions and the same weights, which is what makes them look like the same object stored separately for presentational reasons | If they are genuinely scored differently (different dimensions or weights), a single register with one scoring model produces incomparable numbers side by side, and the quadrant mixes two populations | Ask the engagement lead why they were in a separate sheet and whether the scores were intended to be comparable. Ten minutes. This is Q-05 |
| A-11 | One primary `MaturityAssessment` per engagement, scored by consultants as independent judgment rather than by client self-assessment | M3's grid, rollups and gap-to-opportunity flow all assume a single authoritative assessment. The reference stated explicitly that its scores were the consultancy's independent judgment from interviews and documentation, not a certification | If clients score themselves, or if two assessments must coexist (client self-assessment against consultant assessment), M3 needs a two-series model, and the gap analysis has two definitions of current state | Ask whether any engagement has run a client self-assessment alongside. One conversation |
| A-12 | The firm will supply, own and maintain branded `.pptx` templates with stable named layouts and placeholders | Every requirement in §9.6 binds to named layouts. Without a maintained template the deck export cannot be brand-correct | Deck export produces off-brand output, consultants rebuild by hand, and §12.5 C5 is refuted for a reason that has nothing to do with the product's logic | Ask the brand or marketing owner whether a maintained master template exists, who owns it, and how often it changes. One conversation. This is Q-10 |
| A-13 | A zero-retention, no-training model deployment is available to the firm for the models the capabilities require | FR-1305 and the whole confidentiality posture depend on it. Client narrative content, interview transcripts and maturity rationale all pass through a model | If it is unavailable, capabilities that send client content must be gated behind per-engagement client permission, several capabilities become unusable on sensitive engagements, and the MVP AI scope shrinks | Check the provider's enterprise terms and the firm's existing agreements. One afternoon |
| A-14 | Workshop output can be captured after the session by import, rather than requiring live in-product facilitation | FR-1253's MVP choice depends on it | If consultants will not do a post-session import step, the hand-carry defect persists and the reconciliation feature has no data | Ask the facilitators whether they would export the board and import it the same evening, and what would stop them. Fifteen minutes |
| A-15 | The retention defaults in FR-1311 (90 days audio, 24 months sources, 7 years deliverables and audit) are defensible pending the firm's own records-retention policy | Retention had to be specified to design the purge mechanism and the data model's lifecycle fields | Actual policy or client contracts may require shorter retention, which changes what evidence remains citable, or longer, which changes storage and exposure | Read the firm's records-retention policy and one client contract's data clauses. One afternoon |
| A-16 | The MVP does not integrate with client systems of record (ITSM, PPM, ERP, finance), and file-based ingestion is sufficient | It removes a large integration surface from the MVP, and the reference engagement's inputs were all documents and spreadsheets rather than system feeds | If clients expect their project portfolio or budget system to feed the roadmap directly, the initiative inventory and budget lines go stale and the product looks like a snapshot tool | Ask whether any prior engagement received a system extract rather than a spreadsheet, and whether anyone asked for a live feed. One conversation |

## 14. Open Questions

| ID | Question | Why it matters | Who should decide | What we assume until it is answered |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q-01 | Are the scoring weights (0.40 / 0.35 / 0.25) and the band thresholds (4.5 / 3.75 / 2.8) firm standards, or per-engagement settings? | It determines whether `ScoringModel` is a firm-level locked standard with engagement overrides requiring approval, or free configuration. It also determines whether cross-engagement calibration, benchmarking and precedent bands mean anything at all | Firm methodology owner, with the assessment leads | Firm-level defaults, versioned, with per-engagement override permitted before the first score is committed and requiring an `EngagementLead` decision thereafter. All weights and thresholds are data, never code |
| Q-02 | When the client's workshop-assigned rank disagrees with the calculated weighted score, which governs, and what happens to the other? | The reference engagement stored both, side by side, with no reconciliation rule, and then warned in writing that the deck's rankings would shift. This is the single most consequential unresolved rule in the observed method, because it decides what the roadmap actually says | Firm methodology owner. It is a method question, not a product question | The calculated score governs the register and the default sequence. The client rank is retained as a separate attributed field. A divergence of more than one band requires a `Decision` recording which governs for that item and why, and unresolved divergences block deliverable issue |
| Q-03 | Is the third horizon bucket called `Sequence Later`, `Defer`, or `Future Horizon`? | The reference engagement used all three for what appears to be the same bucket: the workbook's quadrant formula produced `Sequence Later`, the onsite deck and the recap's theme summary used `Defer`, and the recap's own next-steps list used `Future Horizon`. Three names for one concept is how a taxonomy rots, and it is trivially avoidable | Firm methodology owner. A five-minute decision that must be made once | `Sequence Later` as the canonical label, because it is the one the calculation actually produced, with the other two registered as display aliases so historical artifacts still resolve. Horizon labels are engagement-configurable but drawn from a firm-level list |
| Q-04 | Should the quadrant axes be redefined, given that one quadrant is effectively unreachable? | In the reference register the x-axis was the mean of the financial-impact and strategic-alignment scores and the y-axis was the risk score, both cut at 3.5. Across all 55 scored rows, 43 landed in one quadrant, 35 in another and 19 in a third, and the fourth quadrant, the low-value high-urgency "defend" case that exists precisely to catch risk plays that cannot wait regardless of value, received zero rows. A quadrant that never populates is either a definition error or a threshold error, and either way the exhibit is telling the client something untrue about the shape of the portfolio | Firm methodology owner, with whoever designed the exhibit | The axes and threshold are kept as observed for continuity, but the product makes the problem visible: quadrant occupancy counts are displayed on the exhibit, an empty quadrant is flagged in the `Validation Center`, and the axis definitions and threshold are configuration rather than formula, so the firm can retune once and see the effect across every engagement in seconds |
| Q-05 | Are operating-model opportunities scored on the same model as technology opportunities? | The reference engagement scored 12 operating-model opportunities in a separate sheet, with the same three dimensions and the same weights but a different column layout and its own weight row. If they are the same model, they belong in one register; if not, putting them in one quadrant compares incomparable numbers | Firm methodology owner | Same model, one register, with a `category` field distinguishing them so any exhibit can split them. If the answer is no, the product needs two `ScoringModel` instances per engagement and every rollup needs a stated scope |
| Q-06 | Who sets the maturity target level: the consultant, the client, or a benchmark? | The target level drives the gap, the gap drives opportunity generation, and the gap size drives priority-to-fix. If the client sets targets, the assessment becomes negotiated rather than independent, which changes what the deliverable claims. The reference framework sheet stated that most organizations in the client's revenue band target level 3 and that level 3 was the primary target for most areas, which is a benchmark-informed consultant judgment | Firm methodology owner, with the assessment leads | The consultant sets it as independent judgment, informed by a benchmark where one exists, with the basis recorded per focus area (`consultant judgment`, `benchmark`, `client stated ambition`) so the deliverable can say which |
| Q-07 | Will the firm commit to the anonymization programme, and does it hold the rights, that make precedent-based cost estimation possible? | AI-08 and AI-18 exist only if it does. It is a rights, process and staffing commitment (a `PrecedentSteward` role, a two-person release workflow, and counsel review of client contracts), not an engineering task | Firm leadership, with counsel | Not committed. AI-08 and AI-18 are sequenced to Later, the `PrecedentSource` interface is the only coupling, and no MVP feature depends on the library existing |
| Q-08 | Do clients get live access to the roadmap, or only exported artifacts? | It determines whether M7 and M9 are products or reports, whether client-guest access and stakeholder views are built at all, and whether the "living roadmap" in the methodology's ongoing phase is a real capability or a delivered deck that someone updates by hand | Firm leadership, informed by two client sponsors | Exports only in the MVP. Client-guest access ships in v1.1 with server-side scoped views per FR-1322. The product is designed so that turning client access on requires no change to how content is authored |
| Q-09 | Who owns the roadmap after final delivery: the client, the firm, or a joint governance forum? | It determines whether the product keeps a live engagement open after issue, who can edit, who pays for it, and what the retention and access model looks like at month thirteen. The methodology's ongoing phase presumes continued monitoring, benefits tracking and refresh cycles, but the reference engagement's post-onsite trajectory ran into a follow-on scoping deck rather than into a governance cadence | Firm leadership, as a commercial question | The firm owns the model and the client has read access, with an engagement transitioning to a `Managed` state after issue. M9 is Later, so nothing is built on this yet |
| Q-10 | How is a deck template maintained as the firm's brand changes, and who owns that? | Every deck export binds to named layouts and placeholders. A brand refresh that renames or reorders layouts breaks every bound `SlideSpec`, and byte-identical regeneration of old deliverables requires the old template version to be retained indefinitely | Brand or marketing owner, with the product team | A single owner maintains a versioned template registry. Templates are immutable once used by an issued deliverable, new versions are validated against the full `SlideSpec` catalogue before release (AC-1260.3), and old versions are retained for the life of the deliverables that used them |
| Q-11 | What is the commercial model, given that a tool which shortens a 12-week engagement changes what the firm sells? | This is the largest strategic question in the PRD and it is not an engineering one. If the firm bills for time, a tool that removes weeks of analyst effort reduces revenue on every engagement it improves. The plausible answers point at different products: bill for outcome and keep the efficiency; sell a licence or subscription alongside the engagement; use the tool to win more engagements at the same fee; or use it to sell an ongoing managed roadmap service, which is what the methodology's ongoing phase already describes and what the reference engagement's follow-on scoping deck was reaching for | Firm leadership | The tool is treated as internal delivery leverage that improves quality and win rate rather than as a licensed product, and the MVP is scoped for firm-internal use with client read access. This assumption is load-bearing: if the answer is "licensed product", multi-tenancy, per-tenant keys, a public API, self-service onboarding and client-facing support all move into scope and the roadmap changes materially |
| Q-12 | Is the anchored 1-to-5 scale the only score scale in current use, or is the older 8/7/5/4-style scale still live anywhere? | The reference file set contained a hidden ranking sheet on an incompatible scale that did not reconcile with the visible register. If that older scale is still in use on live engagements, the importer needs a maintained mapping rather than the "import as a separate historical score set" default of AC-1213.2 | Firm methodology owner | The 1-to-5 anchored scale is the only current scale. Anything else imports as a historical `ScoreSet`, excluded from all calculations and exhibits |
| Q-13 | Is effort or t-shirt size a scoring dimension, a sequencing input, or both? | The reference engagement scored on three dimensions that exclude effort, then used a six-point t-shirt scale with defined effort, duration and risk per size as a separate sequencing input, and separately used a three-level small/medium/large effort axis on the hidden heat map. Three treatments of one concept. Whether effort enters the priority score changes every number in the register | Firm methodology owner | Effort is a sequencing and capacity input, never a scoring dimension, and the six-point t-shirt scale is canonical. The three-level scale maps into it as an alias |
| Q-14 | What is the durable identity of an `Opportunity`, and should identifiers be stable across engagements? | The reference registers had no identifier column at all, so identity was the initiative-plus-opportunity text pair, which breaks on any rename, and a hidden sheet used a separate prefixed scheme over a non-reconciling set. FR-1214 mints canonical identifiers, but whether they should be meaningful, human-quotable, or comparable across engagements is a firm decision | Firm methodology owner, with the product team | Opaque internal identifiers with a human-readable per-engagement reference (for example `OPP-014`) shown in the UI and in exports, stable across renames, with every legacy identifier retained as an `ExternalRef`. Identifiers are not comparable across engagements |
| Q-15 | Do the firm's client contracts permit the retention defaults in FR-1311, and do any require shorter retention or data residency in a specific region? | Retention and residency are hard to retrofit. They affect what evidence remains citable years later, whether a deliverable can be regenerated on request, and where the infrastructure runs | Counsel, with the commercial team | The FR-1311 defaults, single-region hosting in the firm's primary jurisdiction, and per-engagement override available for retention but not for residency in the MVP |
| Q-16 | Is the pain-point inventory a first-class entity in its own right, or only a source of `Evidence`? | The reference engagement maintained a numbered pain-point inventory of roughly 53 items and linked opportunities to it by a comma-separated list of numbers in a cell, and the inventory itself was a named deliverable ("pain point and opportunity trackers"). If clients expect a pain-point tracker as an output, it needs its own entity, its own view and its own export, not just a `Finding` type | Firm methodology owner | `Finding` covers it, with a `painPoint` classification, a stable per-engagement reference number, and a dedicated register view and export, so the artifact the client expects still exists without a parallel entity |


## Appendix A. Consolidated entity index

This index was generated mechanically from the assembled document and then curated. A name is listed only where the document actually defines it as a named record or value shape — as an entity heading in §5.2, as a node in an entity-relationship diagram, as a declared structure inside a specification block, or as an explicitly named `record` in requirement prose. Controlled vocabularies and enumerations (§5.3) are deliberately excluded: they are value domains, not entities. No entity has been inferred or invented.

The index deliberately makes no claim about which of these are persisted as first-class tables and which are embedded value shapes. The sections do not state that consistently — some authors declared a structure as `Name {` and others as `type Name = {`, and that difference is a writing style, not a design decision. Settling it is part of the reconciliation work below, not something this index should guess at. The one exception is the AI suggestion payloads, which the specifications do explicitly identify as the `payload` carried on an `AISuggestion` rather than as stored records.

The core data model in §5.2 specifies 39 entities. A further 74 named structures are introduced by individual module and AI-capability sections. Those additions have not been restructured or folded into §5 — reconciling them into the core model is recorded as an open question rather than resolved here, because doing so would change requirements that were written against them.
